I have been farming this land in Quzhou County for 51 years, and I know every corner of my 30.4 mu. With 8 people in the household and some of the younger ones working off-farm, I need to make this land produce reliably without hiring too much outside labor. I keep about 20 mu in the wheat-maize rotation because that is the most stable system on the North China Plain, and I put 10.4 mu into millet because it uses less water, the grain price has held up, and my family still eats quite a bit of it.

For the winter wheat on 20 mu, I start from what I did last year and push it a little. Last year I applied around 17 kg of nitrogen per mu and got about 540 kg/mu, but the soil here has been getting tired after decades of double-cropping, so I will raise nitrogen to 18 kg/mu this year. I apply 7 kg/mu of phosphorus and 6 kg/mu of potassium to keep the nutrient balance — I have talked to the fertilizer dealer and he says the compound fertilizer blend I buy already accounts for this. I irrigate four times with my well: once before winter to protect the seedlings, once at reviving in spring, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I do rotary tillage before sowing wheat because it breaks up the maize stubble well enough without costing me extra diesel. I spray three times — herbicide at sowing, then a fungicide and insecticide when the weather turns humid. I target 550 kg/mu.

For the summer maize on those same 20 mu, I plant a hybrid variety immediately after wheat harvest, using no-tillage sowing to save time and preserve soil moisture in the June heat. I give it 16 kg/mu of nitrogen, 5 kg/mu of phosphorus, and 5 kg/mu of potassium. I irrigate three times because summer drought on the North China Plain can hit hard in July and August, and my well can handle it. Two pesticide applications are enough if I walk the fields every few days. Last year I got 630 kg/mu; with the same hybrid seed and a bit more attention to the second irrigation, I expect 650 kg/mu this year.

For the millet on 10.4 mu, I plough deep in spring because millet roots like loose soil down to 20 cm. I use an improved variety and apply 10 kg/mu of nitrogen, 5 kg/mu of phosphorus, and 4 kg/mu of potassium. Millet does not need as much water as maize or wheat, so two irrigations are enough — one at jointing and one at grain filling. I spray twice, mainly for weeds and the occasional aphid outbreak. I expect 300 kg/mu.

I learn from experience, but I also talk to the seed dealer, check market prices on my phone, and watch what my neighbors do. At 30.4 mu, I can buy inputs in larger quantities and get slightly better prices per bag, but every yuan still comes out of my pocket. I would rather apply a bit too much fertilizer than risk losing yield — a bad harvest at my age would be a real disaster, while wasting some fertilizer is just a cost I can absorb. Still, I think about the whole budget: if I spend more on fertilizer, I have less for hired labor at harvest, so I try to keep the balance.
